A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ProofBench/ProofGrader study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, revised, and added material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original expert annotations of 435 generated proofs, evaluator comparisons and ablations, and best-of-n experiments using 464 additional proofs.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results on weaker generators and evaluators, cutoff-based analyses, rubric-selection outcomes, and grading failures.

M1.justification: ProofGrader retains the o3 backbone, reference solutions and marking schemes, NORM instructions, and five-run ensembling. The evaluator prompts and selected rubric-generation prompt are unchanged. Appendix J newly documents the few-shot alternative already mentioned in v1's rubric-generator comparison.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds an expert-graded corpus of proofs from Qwen3-4B and DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, extending the evaluated input population to weaker generators whose outputs are predominantly incorrect. The six competition families and proof-grading task remain unchanged; the cutoff partitions themselves do not add coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-235B-A22B and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct as evaluated grading comparators in Table 14. Table 5 also extends the single-pass versus two-step comparison to R1, which previously appeared only in other experiments. The original evaluator and best-of-n comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce cutoff-based partitions and a 36-problem evaluation of weaker generators. Section 4 changes the stated oracle and mean baselines from the first n candidates to sampled candidates and specifies averaging knockout scores over random brackets. Double-grading coverage changes from 40% to 41%. These are reported setting changes; they do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds competition/year cutoff analyses, weaker-model checks, and a 50-solution failure analysis with detailed over-crediting and under-crediting case studies (Appendices D and F–H). This substantially broadens scrutiny of evaluator reliability. The original rubric-sensitivity experiment and 20-case context-disagreement analysis are retained, with the latter moved into Appendix H.

E5.justification: v1's Table 9, containing 10,000-sample bootstrap confidence intervals and p-values for same-generator versus cross-generator MAE, is removed. The context analysis also loses its reported t-test statistic and associated p-value. Table 1's 95% confidence intervals and Table 4's five-run mean and standard deviation reporting remain.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include per-generator bias, R1 two-step grading, cutoff comparisons, weaker-model evaluations, and failure frequencies. ProofGrader reports MAE 0.431 on the new weaker-generator corpus; its original MAE 0.926 and best-of-16 score 4.14 remain unchanged. Figure 3's overall mean changes from 2.41 to 2.38. The unspecified agreement claim of at least 90% becomes 87.5% within-one-point agreement, which is not a directly comparable agreement measure.

T1.justification: The configuration-selection objective, evaluation metric definitions, Kendall's tau-b formulation, and macroaveraging equations are retained. The additional worked proof in Appendix J serves as a prompting example; it introduces no theoretical result or guarantee for the evaluation methodology.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain ProofBench, a systematic evaluator-design study yielding ProofGrader, and demonstrated best-of-n utility. The abstract retains the same headline accuracy and selection claims. Condensed introduction and conclusion wording does not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of applicability and failure: weaker generators are easier to grade because they mostly produce zero-point proofs; open evaluators lag stronger proprietary models; and ProofGrader can reward superficial rubric alignment, overlook fatal errors, or over-penalize valid progress. It also introduces contamination/generalization interpretations and detailed expert criticism of generated rubrics. These extend beyond v1's existing context and rubric-alignment explanations.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C substantially expand data provenance and annotation documentation, including named rubric-generation models, pilot sizes, rating criteria, annotator assignments, optional AI judgments, and disagreement adjudication. Appendix J supplies the previously undocumented few-shot prompt. These are disclosures, not established procedural changes. The dataset link remains, while code-release wording changes from a present-tense release statement to a publication-time promise.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of NaturalProver and Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT, plus model-documentation references. It removes several rubric-evaluation citations and the dedicated reward-model evaluation subsection. The related-work summary shifts emphasis toward scalable rubric-driven annotation, while the broader positioning around fine-grained natural-language proof evaluation remains.

P1.justification: v2 tightens the dataset description, best-of-n discussion, related work, and conclusion while preserving the main section sequence and much of the prose. It moves detailed context analysis to Appendix H, organizes the expanded appendices as A–K, and adds acknowledgements, ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements. Most prompt text remains verbatim.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is extensively redrawn and rearranged, including replacement of the aggregate model boxplot with cutoff-based comparisons. Table 3 gains bias columns and highlighting, Table 5 gains R1 rows, and Table 7 gains sources. v2 adds six experimental tables and a rubric-annotation interface figure, removes the bootstrap table, and relocates the retained rubric-sensitivity table.

improvement.justification: The expanded annotation documentation, weaker-model checks, and concrete failure cases improve transparency and help readers assess reliability while preserving the main findings. These gains are tempered by removal of bootstrap significance evidence and weaknesses in the new contamination analysis, including conflicting EGMO year counts in Tables 8 and 9 and contamination interpretations based on cutoff comparisons. The net quality improvement is limited.
